FULL VIEW

Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Understand the anatomy of the hindfoot.
Understand common pathologies of the hindfoot that lead to hindfoot deformity and arthritis.
dentify appropriate surgical and nonsurgical treatment options for the management of
hindfoot arthritis.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Hindfoot arthritis may be caused by various pathologies and may result in deformity and
pain. The hindfoot consists of the subtalar, talonavicular, and calcaneocuboid joints.





Nonsurgical and surgical treatment options are available, including bracing, orthotics,
shoewear modifications, injections, and arthrodesis.
Overview
The hindfoot articulations include the subtalar, talonavicular, and calcaneocuboid joints
(Figure 1).
Figure 1 AP (A), lateral (B), and oblique (C) foot and ankle radiographs demonstrate the hindfoot
articulations (arrows), including the subtalar, talonavicular, and calcaneocuboid joints. (Courtesy
of Amanda J. Fantry, MD, Bloomfield, CT.)
Epidemiology
Arthritis of the hindfoot may result from trauma (calcaneal or talar fractures), inflammatory
disorders, primary osteoarthritis, infection, osteonecrosis, end-stage posterior tibial tendon
dysfunction, tarsal coalitions, and neurologic disorders associated with long-standing
cavovarus foot deformity.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Hindfoot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000011
2/28

Long-standing planovalgus deformity also may lead to hindfoot arthritis. In addition,
congenital conditions, such as tarsal coalition, may result in unilateral or bilateral hindfoot
valgus deformity.
Cavovarus deformities often are associated with inherited motor sensory neuropathies, such
as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease or post-polio syndromes.
Isolated talonavicular joint arthritis may be associated with inflammatory arthropathy, such as
rheumatoid arthritis, osteonecrosis of the navicular, or trauma.

Epidemiology
Hindfoot arthritis may occur posttraumatically or result from various other etiologies,
including congenital conditions, posterior tibial tendon dysfunction, inflammatory
arthropathy, and neurological dysfunction. Deformities may be varus, with or without
cavus deformity, or planovalgus.
Anatomy and Biomechanics

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The hindfoot joints (subtalar, talonavicular, and calcaneocuboid) consists of four bones:
the calcaneus, talus, navicular, and cuboid. Hindfoot motion simply can be described as
eversion and inversion, which allows for accommodation on uneven ground and
transitions from eversion to inversion throughout gait. The axis of the subtalar joint runs
obliquely from plantar lateral to dorsomedial. This obliquity has led to the subtalar joint
being compared to a mitered hinge, such that the foot rotates outward with dorsiflexion
and inward with plantar flexion (Figure 2).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Hindfoot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000011
3/28

Figure 2 Illustration shows that, with the leg fixed in position and the foot free, the
oblique ankle joint axis causes outward rotation with dorsiflexion and inward rotation
with plantar flexion (Reproduced with permission from Haskell A, Mann RA:
Biomechanics of the foot and ankle, in Coughlin MJ, Saltzman CL, Anderson RB eds:
Mann’s Surgery of the Foot and Ankle, ed 9. Philadelphia, PA, Saunders, 2014, pp 3-36.)
The posterior tibial tendon is responsible for inversion and is the predominant stabilizer
of the longitudinal arch. If the posterior tibial tendon fails, the longitudinal arch will
collapse, and the hindfoot will deform into valgus. The posterior tibial tendon inserts
onto the navicular tuberosity.
The peroneal tendons are responsible for plantar flexion of the first ray (peroneus
longus) and eversion of the hindfoot (peroneus brevis and longus). The peroneus brevis
inserts onto the fifth metatarsal base and the peroneus longus inserts onto the plantar
base of the medial cuneiform and the first ray.
With increasing deformity, the medial and lateral ligamentous complexes may be
affected. In cavovarus deformity, the lateral ligaments may attenuate over time, leading
to lateral instability clinically and radiographically. The deltoid may fail with progressive
planovalgus deformity and cause valgus ankle arthritis (stage IV acquired adult flatfoot
disorder).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Hindfoot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000011
4/28

Osteology
The hindfoot consists of four bones (calcaneus, talus, cuboid, and navicular) and three
articulations (the subtalar, talonavicular, and calcaneocuboid joints).
The hindfoot joints allow for eversion and inversion. This facilitates walking on uneven ground.
The axis of the subtalar joint is oriented approximately 40° upward from the axial plane and
20° medially from the midline.
The hindfoot progresses from maximal eversion during the initial phase of stance/heel strike
to progressive inversion at toe-off. With eversion, the hindfoot is supple and serves as a shock
absorber. With inversion, the foot is more rigid and serves as a stable platform for push-off.
Nerves
The peroneal tendons are not directly innervated by any nerve. They are composed of fibrous
tissue and primarily function to transmit the contractile force of the peroneus longus and
brevis muscles to the foot.
The sural nerve courses posterior to the peroneal tendons at the level of the ankle. While it
travels along the lateral aspect of the foot, it doesn't actually cross over the top of the peroneal
tendons. Instead, it runs alongside them towards the heel and provides sensory innervation to
the lateral side of the foot.
The posterior tibial tendon is innervated by the tibial nerve.
Tendons
Posterior tibial tendon
The posterior tibialis muscle originates from the interosseous membrane at the proximal
one-third of the leg and becomes tendinous at the distal one-third. It courses directly
posterior to the medial malleolus.
It inserts predominantly in the navicular tuberosity but has multiple other bony insertions.
It is responsible for inversion of the subtalar joint.
The posterior tibial tendon is the predominant stabilizer of the longitudinal arch.
Peroneal tendons
Peroneus longus: originates at the lateral condyle of the tibia and the head of the fibula and
inserts on the plantar aspect of the medial cuneiform and the first ray
Courses posterior to the peroneus brevis at the level of the ankle
Responsible for plantar flexion of the first ray and eversion of the hindfoot
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Hindfoot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000011
5/28

Primary antagonist is the anterior tibial tendon
Peroneus brevis: originates from the midportion of the lateral fibula and inserts onto the
base of the fifth metatarsal
Responsible for eversion and plantar flexion of the foot
Joints and Ligaments
The deltoid ligament is involved in late-stage (stage IV) flatfoot deformity as increasing valgus
load creates valgus tilt through the ankle and attenuation of the deltoid
The lateral ankle ligaments (anterior talofibular ligament and calcaneofibular ligament) may be
affected in patients with varus hindfoot pathology, leading to ligamentous laxity.
Etiology
Hindfoot arthritis develops in a manner similar to arthritis affecting other joints. It is the result
of direct cartilage or chondrocyte damage from acute microtrauma, repetitive microtrauma,
abnormal weight-bearing stress from articular incongruity, joint malalignment, adjacent joint
arthrodesis, or increased shear stress from ligamentous instability (Figure 3; Resource 1).

in Chou LB, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Foot and Ankle, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American

Posttraumatic arthritis
Calcaneal fractures (Figure 4)
Calcaneal malunion may lead to a shortened, depressed, and varus heel deformity with
resultant subtalar arthritis.
Patients typically report pain at the sinus tarsi.
They also may report anterior ankle impingement and decreased ankle motion with
considerable subtalar joint depression.

calcaneal fracture. B, Lateral radiograph demonstrates initial management via open reduction
and internal fixation. C, Radiograph demonstrates loss of calcaneal height and subtalar arthritis

Talar fractures
Malunion of talar fractures or disruption of vascular supply and the development of
osteonecrosis may lead to tibiotalar and/or subtalar arthritis.
Inflammatory arthritis
Typically related to long-standing disease
Joint destruction occurring from synovial inflammation and cartilage erosion in combination
with soft-tissue disease, including possible tendon rupture
Planovalgus deformity secondary to instability of the subtalar and transverse tarsal joints
observed in patients with rheumatoid arthritis
Tarsal coalition: talocalcaneal, calcaneonavicular
Failure of mesenchymal segmentation
Often present in patients aged 8 to 15 years (Figure 5)

Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction (Figure 6)

Charcot arthropathy
Talonavicular arthritis (Figure 8)
Müller-Weiss disease
Deformity, sclerosis, and often necrosis of the navicular, leading to a comma-shaped
navicular with collapse of the lateral aspect
Typically occurs in patients aged 40 to 60 years
Posttraumatic
Rheumatoid arthritis

Figure 8 Preoperative lateral (A), postoperative lateral (B), preoperative AP (C), and postoperative

Eckel TT, Shawen SB: Hindfoot arthritis, in Chou LB, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Foot and


Etiology
No one cause of hindfoot deformity exists, and various pathologies may contribute to
hindfoot varus or valgus deformities. Calcaneal fractures may result in subtalar arthritis
because of damage to the articular cartilage from the initial injury, and calcaneal
malunions frequently result in a shortened, varus, and depressed calcaneus. Isolated
subtalar arthritis often results in pain at the sinus tarsi. Talar fractures may result in
tibiotalar or subtalar arthritis.
Commonly, posterior tibial tendon dysfunction will lead to increased hindfoot valgus,
which will cause increased stress across the medial hindfoot and may worsen deformity
over time. Planovalgus deformity also may result from rheumatoid arthritis and collapse
of the hindfoot and the transverse tarsal joints. Patients with congenital disorders, such
as coalition, may present with fixed hindfoot valgus and are commonly identified
between the ages 8 to 15 years.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Hindfoot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000011
11/28

Cavovarus deformity may result from congenital disorders, such as congenital hereditary
motor sensory neuropathies (eg, polio or Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease).
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Trauma/mechanism of injury (high or low energy)
Previous surgery
Insidious or sudden onset
Start-up pain common
Patients often report increasing deformity that is worsening over time.
Pain often is worse with uneven ground because the tendons (posterior tibial tendon,
peroneal tendons) and joints (subtalar and Chopart joints) are responsible for accommodating
uneven surfaces

Patient History
Obtaining an accurate and detailed patient history is paramount to determining the
pathology of hindfoot deformities and arthritis because of the numerous possible
etiologies. Surgeons should ask about previous trauma and surgeries, family history of
heritable conditions (such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease), and deformity progression
over time. Patients with associated tendon disorders may report pain over the posterior
tibial tendon or peroneal tendons. With increasing planovalgus deformity, the talar head
may become palpable or an ulceration may develop. Similarly, with increasing cavovarus
deformity, callus or ulceration may develop over the fifth metatarsal base. Patients often
report increasing pain on uneven ground.
Physical Examination
Standing examination to evaluate hindfoot alignment (Figure 9)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Hindfoot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000011
12/28

Evaluate lower-extremity alignment (eg, genu valgus or varum as a contributor to
malalignment at the hindfoot)
Figure 9 Clinical photograph of bilateral feet and ankles shows increased hindfoot valgus noted
on standing examination, with the too-many-toes sign observed on the right side. (Courtesy of
Amanda J. Fantry, MD, Bloomfield, CT.)
Single-limb heel raise (abnormal with posterior tibial tendon dysfunction)
Gait examination
Evaluate fixed versus flexible deformities
Evaluate strength of the peroneal, tibialis anterior, and posterior tibial tendons and pain with
resisted motor testing
Palpation of the peroneal tendons, posterior tibial tendon, sinus tarsi/subtalar joint,
calcaneocuboid joint, talonavicular joint, and tibiotalar joint for swelling and tenderness
Pain with passive/active inversion and eversion
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000011
13/28

Coalition patients have pain at the site of the coalition and limited passive hindfoot range of
motion.
Evaluate for equinus deformity: gastrocnemius contracture or combined gastrocsoleus
contracture
Perform a Silfverskiöld test
Coleman block test
Can establish if hindfoot varus is forefoot- or hindfoot-driven and help determine flexibility of
the deformity

Physical Examination
Patients need to be evaluated in a standing position, with the patient facing toward and
away from the surgeon. The position of the hindfoot and lower extremity alignment
(genu varum or valgus, tibial deformity) should be evaluated. A gait examination should
be performed. If concern for acquired adult flatfoot deformity exists, the patient should
perform a single-limb heel rise, which should be compared with that on the unaffected
side. The Coleman block test may be performed in patients with hindfoot varus in whom
the pathology (hindfoot versus forefoot pathology) is unclear.
On seated examination, areas of tenderness should be palpated, including over the
hindfoot joints, posterior tibial tendon, and peroneal tendons. The ankle should be
evaluated for ligament instability. Resisted motor strength testing should be performed
in inversion and eversion. Surgeons should determine if the deformities are fixed (not
passively correctable) versus flexible because it will influence treatment options.
A Silfverskiöld test will help determine if a gastrocnemius contracture also is present.
Gastrocnemius contractures are very common in patients with a hindfoot deformity
because the biomechanical axis of the Achilles tendon is no longer in line with the
anatomic axis of the ankle joint.
Neurovascular Examination
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Hindfoot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000011
14/28

Standard neurovascular examination, including pulses of the deep peroneal and posterior
tibial arteries
Referral for vascular studies if pulses are not palpable
Sensory testing of all nerve distributions of the foot may help identify early neuropathy.
Motor testing of toe flexors and extensors, ankle inversion (posterior tibial tendon) and
eversion (peroneal tendons), ankle dorsiflexion (tibialis anterior), and plantar flexion
(gastrocsoleus)

Neurovascular Examination
A thorough neurovascular examination, including motor function, and sensory
examination must be performed. Semmes-Weinstein monofilament may be used to
identify neuropathy. Lack of pedal pulses frequently necessitates referral to vascular
surgery.
Imaging Studies

Imaging Studies
Five weight-bearing radiographs of the foot and ankle should be obtained. An AP
radiograph can be obtained to determine abduction through the Chopart (talonavicular
and calcaneocuboid) joints, which is commonly observed in patients with adult acquired
flatfoot deformity. Oblique radiographs will help identify pathology at the
calcaneocuboid joint or calcaneonavicular or lateral talonavicular joints, such as a
coalition. Lateral radiographs may be used to identify cavus deformity with increased
calcaneal inclination, an abnormal talo-first metatarsal angle (Meary line), stacking of the
metatarsals, and stacking of the navicular on the cuboid. In patients with a planovalgus
foot, collapse of the Meary talo-first metatarsal angle will be observed. Ankle
radiographs will help determine if contributing deformity or abnormality through the
tibiotalar joint is present.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Hindfoot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000011
15/28

Special views, including Broden, Harris, and Saltzman views, may aid in determining
alignment and pathology.
CT and MRI often are unnecessary in patients with hindfoot arthritides but may be
helpful for preoperative planning, determining whether a coalition is present, or
tendinous evaluation.
Radiography
Five weight-bearing views of the foot and ankle
AP: identify degenerative conditions of the talonavicular and forefoot abduction/adduction
Oblique: identify degenerative changes at the calcaneocuboid joint and the lateral
talonavicular
Lateral view
Evaluate the lateral talar–first metatarsal angle (Meary line)
Identify planus or cavus deformities
Ankle radiographs
Identify any tibiotalar deformity
Specialized views
Broden view: can visualize the posterior facet of the subtalar joint
Harris view: axial view of the calcaneus
Saltzmann view: tangential PA view of the leg and ankle to evaluate hindfoot alignment
Computed Tomography
Weight-bearing CT if possible
Frequently unnecessary for diagnostic purposes but may aid in preoperative planning
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Used to evaluate tendinous and ligamentous structures (posterior tibial tendon, spring
ligament, peroneal tendons) if necessary
Can detect concomitant insufficiency fractures
If planning fusion surgery for the management of rigid deformity, MRI often is unnecessary.

16/28

May aid in identifying a fibrous coalition
Diagnosis
Identify joint involvement (multiple or single joints of the hindfoot), with or without ankle joint
involvement
Identify predominant deformity (varus or valgus through the hindfoot)
Management
Nonsurgical Management
NSAIDs
Activity modifications
Avoid high-impact activities
Avoid uneven terrain
Shoe modifications
If deformity is flexible, custom or over-the-counter orthotics may be considered, particularly
for valgus deformity. Appropriate posting is determined by the nature of deformity.
Fixed deformities require accommodative orthotics to more evenly distribute ground
reaction forces and prevent skin breakdown.
Rocker-bottom shoes may alleviate pain by decreasing push-off forces through the
transverse tarsal joints.
Bracing management that protects the hindfoot
University of California Biomechanics Laboratory orthosis
Ankle-foot orthosis brace
Arizona brace
Corticosteroid injections
Selective (fluoroscopically guided) anesthetic/corticosteroid injections occasionally are
therapeutic; however, they typically are used to identify the symptomatic hindfoot
articulations.

Nonsurgical Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Hindfoot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000011
17/28

Activity modifications, including avoiding uneven terrain and high-impact activities, are
easy suggestions to improve mild symptoms. Flexible deformities often are amenable to
bracing and orthotics, particularly in patients with valgus deformity. Bracing and
orthotics may be available over the counter or custom, depending on the degree of
deformity and correction desired. Bracing, including a Richie brace, ankle-foot orthosis,
or Arizona brace, may be considered. Fixed deformities often require custom orthotics
or bracing designed to offload areas of increased pressure and minimize pain.
Corticosteroid injections may be used selectively to improve pain or identify involved
joints.
Surgical Management
Indications
Chronic hindfoot pain with associated degenerative/posttraumatic disease of the hindfoot
Recalcitrant inflammatory arthropathy of the hindfoot
Symptomatic or previously resected coalition
Failed nonsurgical management, including anti-inflammatories, shoe modifications, orthotics,
and bracing

Indications
Surgical management should be considered in patients in whom nonsurgical
management, including anti-inflammatory medications, bracing, and a course of
immobilization fails and who continue to experience pain associated with the hindfoot.
This includes patients with severe hindfoot deformity, particularly those at risk for
ulceration; patients with a coalition in whom prior resection failed or who are
symptomatic; and patients who have pain associated with the hindfoot deformity that is
consistent with the history and physical examination.
Contraindications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Hindfoot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000011
18/28

Active infection
Poorly controlled diabetes mellitus (in patients without ulcers or indications for more urgent
surgical treatment)
Medical comorbidities associated with severe wound-healing risks
Inability to remain non–weight bearing postoperatively
Severe peripheral vascular disease
Recommend referral to a vascular surgeon
Smoking/nicotine use (relative contraindication)

Contraindications
Contraindications to surgical management include poorly controlled diabetes mellitus;
however, this is relative because ulceration or impending ulceration in patients with
diabetes mellitus may necessitate management. Other contraindications include severe
peripheral vascular disease, medical comorbidities that preclude surgical management,
and smoking status/nicotine use.
Techniques/Procedures
Very few indications for arthrotomy or arthroscopy for the management of hindfoot arthritis,
but it can be performed to remove symptomatic exostoses
Arthrodesis is the mainstay of the surgical management of hindfoot arthritis.
Can selectively fuse joints of the hindfoot, depending on pathology
Fusing joints of the hindfoot decreases motion, with isolated fusions limiting motion 25% for
calcaneocuboid fusions, 40% for subtalar fusion, and more than 90% for talonavicular
fusions
Frequently, fusion of the subtalar and talonavicular joints is performed in combination
because fusion of the talonavicular joint eliminates almost all subtalar motion
Triple arthrodesis often is performed in combination with gastrocnemius recession because
long-standing gastrocnemius contracture occurs secondary to the valgus deformity and
medialized position of the Achilles tendon.
Triple arthrodesis can be performed via two incisions (medial to the talonavicular joint and
lateral to the subtalar/calcaneocuboid joints) or via a single, medial incision (Figure 10).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Hindfoot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000011
19/28

A single, medial approach is beneficial in patients with advanced valgus deformity in
whom contracted lateral soft tissues may lead to wound healing issues.
Increased risk for disruption of talar blood supply and risk to the deltoid ligament
In addition, a single medial approach may lead to inadequate deformity correction
because of lack of balanced visualization of the foot and inadequate joint preparation for
fusion (most common residual deformity is fixed supination and lateral column overload).
Fusion rates of a triple arthrodesis are approximately 95%.
Concern for adjacent joint arthritis, primarily at the ankle joint and naviculocuneiform
joints
Calcaneal malunion may result in loss of height, limitations in ankle motion, and subtalar
arthritis.
Bone-block arthrodesis may restore height and increase calcaneal inclination.
Wound-healing risk with increasing bone-block height
Often need to perform a lateral wall exostectomy to improve subfibular impingement
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Hindfoot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000011
20/28

Figure 10 Radiographs of a foot demonstrate triple arthrodesis. Preoperative AP (A) and lateral
(B) radiographs demonstrate a fixed planovalgus deformity. Postoperative AP (C) and lateral (D)
radiographs demonstrate triple arthrodesis. (Reproduced from Eckel TT, Shawen SB: Hindfoot
arthritis, in Chou LB, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Foot and Ankle, ed 5. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2014, pp 145-157.)

Techniques/Procedures
The mainstay of surgical treatment for hindfoot arthritis is arthrodesis. Fusion of the
hindfoot will decrease motion, with isolated single joint fusion limiting motion less than
double or triple arthrodesis. A talonavicular fusion alone will eliminate almost all
hindfoot motion and often is combined with subtalar fusion (frequently referred to as
double arthrodesis). Triple arthrodesis (subtalar, talonavicular, and calcaneocuboid
fusion) is associated with a fusion rate greater than 90%. Hindfoot fusions often are
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Hindfoot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000011
21/28

combined with gastrocnemius recession because it often is required to create a
plantigrade foot intraoperatively.
Isolated subtalar fusion often is performed for posttraumatic arthritis after a calcaneal
fracture, talocalcaneal coalitions, and some deformities that may be corrected through
the subtalar joint alone. Bone block arthrodesis may be considered for substantial loss
of calcaneal height; however, this poses a wound healing risk.
Preoperative Planning
Determine which joints are symptomatic and what deformity requires correction (ie, isolated
subtalar arthritis in a patient with a calcaneal fracture versus a fixed planovalgus deformity;
Figure 11)
Determine if adjunct procedures of the midfoot/forefoot may be necessary
Determine if soft-tissue procedures (tendon lengthening/transfers, capsular releases) may be
necessary for deformity correction
Figure 11 AP (A), oblique (B), and lateral (C) radiographs of a foot demonstrate a planovalgus
deformity, with subluxation of the talonavicular joint and increased talar declination. Joint space
narrowing and subchondral cyst formation are observed at the talonavicular and calcaneocuboid
joints. (Courtesy of Amanda J. Fantry, MD, Bloomfield, CT.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Hindfoot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000011
22/28


Preoperative Planning
Surgeons must determine what joints are involved and how to best correct hindfoot
pathology and deformity. This may be accomplished via fusion of one or multiple joints.
Adjunct procedures, including those through the midfoot or forefoot, and soft-tissue
procedures, including lengthening or transfer of the tendons, may be necessary to
achieve a plantigrade foot.
Anesthesia and Patient Positioning
Anesthesia
General
Popliteal and saphenous nerve block
Supine patient positioning
Can elevate surgical extremity on bone ramp
Bump under the ipsilateral hip to get the toes to point directly to the ceiling
Surgical Approaches
Approach to the subtalar joint
Sinus tarsi approach from the tip of the fibula in line with the fourth metatarsal
The sural nerve should be inferior to the dissection; always look for it.
Elevate the extensor digitorum brevis dorsally.
Can continue the approach distally to the calcaneocuboid joint if necessary
For severe valgus, a medial approach to the talonavicular and subtalar joint has been used.
Instrumentation
Solid or cannulated screws
Usually 5.5 mm or larger
If using headed screws, ensure they will not impede ankle range of motion and are not on
the weight-bearing surface of the calcaneus.
Approach to the talonavicular joint
Dorsal approach between the tibialis anterior and the extensor hallucis longus tendons;
protect the neurovascular bundle
Can use cannulated screws, compression plating, or staples

Can use a lamina spreader in the subtalar joint; ensure all articular cartilage is removed
throughout the anterior, middle, and posterior facets
Use a combination of osteotomes, burr, curets, and rongeur
Can place a spring distractor in the talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints

Joint positioning
Goal is to create a plantigrade foot with re-establishment of the Meary talo-first metatarsal
line (a radiographic line through the talus and the first metatarsal head) on an AP view of the
foot and a lateral view of the ankle
Hindfoot alignment
If performing triple arthrodesis or subtalar arthrodesis, the subtalar joint must be
positioned in approximately 5° of hindfoot valgus.
Can correct the talonavicular or the subtalar joint first
Position the Chopart joints to rotate the foot out of supination and abduction (in
planovalgus deformity)
Fuse the calcaneocuboid joint last. May apply upward (dorsal) pressure on the cuboid to
ensure it does not sublux plantarly and create lateral column overload with gait
Can use solid screws, cannulated screws, compression plates, or staples
Evaluate alignment of the forefoot after hindfoot fusion to ensure the forefoot is not
supinated; a forefoot osteotomy may be required for correction.
Consider the need for soft-tissue releases or lengthening

Fusion of the hindfoot often is performed with the patient in the supine position;
however, the patient may be positioned laterally. The goal of arthrodesis is to achieve
osseous union, and surgeons must maintain principles, including adequate joint
preparation, deformity correction to a plantigrade foot, and compression across the
fusion surfaces.
The subtalar joint and the calcaneocuboid joint may be approached via a sinus tarsi
incision that is extended distally to the calcaneocuboid joint. The talonavicular joint may
be approached medially or dorsomedially. Distractors, including lamina spreaders or
small joint distractors, may be used to adequately visualize the articular surfaces and
ensure appropriate joint preparation.
After joint preparation, the hindfoot is positioned in approximately 5° of hindfoot valgus.
Additional soft-tissue procedures or releases may be necessary to achieve this. Most
commonly, the subtalar joint is fixed first, with multiple options available for screw
placement (from the talar neck into the calcaneus or from the plantar calcaneus to the
talus). In triple arthrodesis, the Chopart joints need to be pronated and adducted to
prevent overload of the lateral column after correction of hindfoot valgus through the
subtalar joint.
Multiple fixation options, including cannulated or solid screws, staples, or compression
plating, can be used. A hindfoot fusion nail may be used if concomitant tibiotalar joint
pathology is present.
Postoperative Management
Initial postoperative splint
Suture removal at approximately 2 weeks postoperatively
Transition to a cast or boot at that time
No weight bearing for at least 6 weeks postoperatively
CT scan appropriate to confirm successful arthrodesis before unrestricted weight bearing
Deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis evaluation is important.

Postoperative Management
A splint is used for immobilization, with plans to remove sutures at approximately 10 to
20 days postoperatively. Weight bearing frequently is not allowed for 6 to 12 weeks,
depending on surgeon preference and associated comorbidities. Deep vein thrombosis
prophylaxis is recommended for at least 30 days postoperatively, depending on surgeon
preference.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Adequate joint preparation is the most important for fusion.
Identify any crossing branches of the sural nerve.
Isolated arthrodesis of the talonavicular joint is associated with a higher nonunion rate and
may result in an adducted foot.
Ensure the position of the first ray is addressed after correction of the hindfoot for any
additional procedures that may be necessary.
Complications
Malunion
Approximately 3%
Most common deformity: equinovarus
Nonunion
After triple arthrodesis: 3% to 17%
Superficial wound complication: 3% to 30%
Deep infection
Adjacent joint arthritis
Midfoot arthritis develops in 30% to 50% of patients after triple arthrodesis.
Talonavicular/calcaneocuboid arthritis may occur after isolated subtalar arthritis
Thromboembolic disease
Nerve complications, including neuroma, neuralgia, complex regional pain syndrome
Sural nerve injury with calcaneocuboid arthritis most common (as high as 32%)

Complications
Postoperative complications, including superficial and deep wound infections, may
require oral antibiotic agents, a return to the operating room, or intravenous antibiotic
agents. Nonunion rates vary from 3% to 17% in patients who undergo triple arthrodesis.
Adjacent joint arthritis, including midfoot arthritis, may develop after triple, and arthritic
changes may occur at the Chopart joints after subtalar fusion. The sural nerve is the
most commonly injured nerve in the hindfoot, and care must be taken to protect this
nerve intraoperatively. More serious nerve complications, including complex regional
pain syndrome, can occur.
Outcomes
Union rates for subtalar arthrodesis are approximately 85% to 100%
Union rates for triple arthrodesis range from 83% to 97%
